Getting started with pedkindraw

Source: vignettes/pedkindraw.Rmd
pedkindraw.Rmd

This vignette takes one pedigree from its records to a drawing. It reads the example pedigree that comes with the package, checks it, numbers its generations and family trees, computes kinship, trims it to one animal’s ancestors and draws them. Then it shrinks the pedigree and finds a set of unrelated animals in it. The last section converts a kinship2 pedigree.

A pedigree is a data frame

A pedigree has one row per animal: its id, sire and dam (NA for an unknown parent; an animal may have one known parent), and optionally its sex ("M", "F", "H" for a hermaphrodite or "U" for unknown), a status ("DECEASED" marks an animal that has died) and condition columns, whose names start with affected. Other columns are kept. Twins are listed in a table of their own, one pair per row: id1, id2 and code ("MZ twin", "DZ twin" or "UZ twin", for identical, fraternal and unknown).

pedkindraw comes with a pedigree of 375 rhesus macaques and the table of its three twin pairs. Both are files copied unchanged from the examples of the package nprcgenekeepr, which disguised (obfuscated) the records for use in examples.

library(pedkindraw)

pedFile <- system.file("extdata", "obfuscated_rhesus_mhc_ped.csv",
                       package = "pedkindraw")
twinFile <- system.file("extdata", "obfuscated_rhesus_mhc_twin_relations.csv",
                        package = "pedkindraw")
ped <- read.csv(pedFile, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
twins <- read.csv(twinFile, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
nrow(ped)
#> [1] 375
head(ped)
#>       id sire  dam sex gen      birth exit  age
#> 1 BRI2MW <NA> <NA>   F   0 1998-12-06   NA 20.7
#> 2 677E7M <NA> <NA>   F   0 1998-07-24   NA 21.1
#> 3 ZZ646X <NA> <NA>   F   0 1997-12-08   NA 21.7
#> 4 FEEN9W <NA> <NA>   M   0 1997-12-23   NA 21.7
#> 5 83U0EX <NA> <NA>   M   0       <NA>   NA   NA
#> 6 6VUC6R <NA> <NA>   F   0       <NA>   NA   NA
twins
#>      id1    id2    code
#> 1 E06FRB HV7LZ3 MZ twin
#> 2 8GSXTQ P844CW DZ twin
#> 3 BRI2MW 677E7M UZ twin

Besides id, sire, dam and sex, the file gives each animal’s generation (gen), birth date, exit date and age. It has no status or condition column, so the drawing below marks neither.

Checking the records

checkPedigree() lists each problem it finds, one row per problem, and changes nothing. It finds none in the example. checkTwinRelations() stops if a twin pair is not possible, for instance MZ or DZ twins that do not share a sire and a dam, and otherwise returns the table.

checkPedigree(ped)
#> [1] check  id     detail
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
twins <- checkTwinRelations(ped, twins)

Records with problems look like this. Here s2 is the sire of o2 but has no row of its own, and d1, the dam of o1 and o2, is recorded as male.

records <- data.frame(
  id   = c("s1", "d1", "o1", "o2"),
  sire = c(NA, NA, "s1", "s2"),
  dam  = c(NA, NA, "d1", "d1"),
  sex  = c("M", "M", "F", "M")
)
checkPedigree(records)
#>            check id        detail
#> 1 rowlessParents s2    sire of o2
#> 2       maleDams d1 dam of o1, o2

addParents() adds a row for each sire or dam that has none, and marks the rows in a recordStatus column. correctParentSex() sets the sex of each sire recorded as female and each dam recorded as male. After both, the check finds nothing.

records <- addParents(records)
records$sex <- correctParentSex(records$id, records$sire, records$dam,
                                records$sex, records$recordStatus)
records
#>   id sire  dam sex recordStatus
#> 1 s1 <NA> <NA>   M     original
#> 2 d1 <NA> <NA>   F     original
#> 3 o1   s1   d1   F     original
#> 4 o2   s2   d1   M     original
#> 5 s2 <NA> <NA>   M        added
checkPedigree(records)
#> [1] check  id     detail
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

Generations and family trees

findGeneration() numbers each animal’s generation: 0 for a founder, an animal with no known sire or dam, and one more than its later parent’s for every other. The layout and kinship() need these numbers. The example spans nine generations, 0 to 8, and the numbers are the same as the file’s own gen column, which this line replaces.

ped$gen <- findGeneration(ped$id, ped$sire, ped$dam)
table(ped$gen)
#> 
#>   0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8 
#> 124  60  46  40  34  29  23  16   3

findPedigreeNumber() numbers the family trees: animals joined through their sires and dams share a number. The example has five trees, one of 343 animals and four of 3 to 13.

ped$family <- findPedigreeNumber(ped$id, ped$sire, ped$dam)
table(ped$family)
#> 
#>   1   2   3   4   5 
#>  11   5   3  13 343

Kinship

kinship() computes the kinship coefficient of every pair of animals: the chance that an allele taken at random from one animal and an allele taken at random from the other are identical by descent. An animal’s coefficient with itself is 0.5, or more when it is inbred. With sparse = TRUE it returns a sparse matrix, which saves memory in a large pedigree.

k <- kinship(ped$id, ped$sire, ped$dam, ped$gen, twinRelations = twins)
dim(k)
#> [1] 375 375
k[c("E06FRB", "HV7LZ3", "8GSXTQ", "P844CW"),
  c("E06FRB", "HV7LZ3", "8GSXTQ", "P844CW")]
#>        E06FRB HV7LZ3 8GSXTQ P844CW
#> E06FRB    0.5    0.5   0.00   0.00
#> HV7LZ3    0.5    0.5   0.00   0.00
#> 8GSXTQ    0.0    0.0   0.50   0.25
#> P844CW    0.0    0.0   0.25   0.50

E06FRB and HV7LZ3 are identical (MZ) twins. The twins table gives them a coefficient of 0.5, the same as each has with itself; without it they would have 0.25, that of full siblings. 8GSXTQ and P844CW are fraternal (DZ) twins, full siblings, at 0.25.

An animal whose sire and dam are related is inbred. The example has 29 such animals.

sum(diag(k) > 0.5)
#> [1] 29
k[c("81MJXH", "H16XSK", "ED5PDV"), c("81MJXH", "H16XSK", "ED5PDV")]
#>        81MJXH H16XSK ED5PDV
#> 81MJXH 0.5000 0.1250 0.3125
#> H16XSK 0.1250 0.5000 0.3125
#> ED5PDV 0.3125 0.3125 0.5625

One of them is ED5PDV. Its sire 81MJXH and its dam H16XSK are half siblings, both offspring of YPHFHF, and their kinship coefficient is 0.125. So ED5PDV’s coefficient with itself is (1 + 0.125) / 2 = 0.5625.

Trimming a pedigree to the animals of interest

getProbandPedigree() keeps the animals of interest, the probands, and all of their ancestors. ED5PDV and its ancestors are 16 animals in five generations, 8 of them founders.

small <- getProbandPedigree(ped, "ED5PDV")
nrow(small)
#> [1] 16

trimPedigree() does the same, and with removeUninformative = TRUE it also removes each founder that has only one offspring, again and again until none is left. Such a founder changes no kinship coefficient among the animals left. Here that leaves the four animals that make ED5PDV inbred: YPHFHF, its offspring 81MJXH and H16XSK, and ED5PDV.

core <- trimPedigree(ped, "ED5PDV", removeUninformative = TRUE)
core[, c("id", "sire", "dam", "sex")]
#>         id   sire    dam sex
#> 204 YPHFHF   <NA>   <NA>   M
#> 237 H16XSK YPHFHF   <NA>   F
#> 252 81MJXH YPHFHF   <NA>   M
#> 301 ED5PDV 81MJXH H16XSK   M

Drawing a pedigree

makePedigreeMatingLayout() places each animal and each mating of a pedigree, and drawPedigreeDiagram() draws the layout as an interactive graph. The layout can also take a twins table, a kinship matrix and layout hints, which its help page describes.

layout <- makePedigreeMatingLayout(small)
drawPedigreeDiagram(layout)

Squares are males and circles females. The small dot between two animals is their mating, and a line goes down from it to each of their offspring. The mating of the half siblings 81MJXH and H16XSK is drawn in orange, because their kinship coefficient is above 0. Three animals are drawn twice, and a dashed line joins the two places of each: YPHFHF beside each of its two mates, and 5LDNWE and H16XSK under their sire and dam and again beside their mate. In the drawing you can zoom, hover over an animal to highlight the animals joined to it, pick an animal in the “Select by id” box, and save the picture with the “Export Diagram (PNG)” button.

Shrinking a pedigree

shrinkPedigree() trims a pedigree to the animals needed to keep it informative within a budget on its bit size, given which animals are genotyped and, optionally, which are affected. It follows kinship2’s pedigree.shrink(). The bit size, which bitSize() gives, is twice the number of animals with a known parent less the number of founders. The example has no genotypes, so 30 percent of the animals are picked at random to stand for the genotyped ones: 109 of the 375.

set.seed(42)
genotyped <- runif(nrow(ped)) < 0.3
sum(genotyped)
#> [1] 109
bitSize(ped)
#> $bitSize
#> [1] 378
#> 
#> $nFounder
#> [1] 124
#> 
#> $nNonFounder
#> [1] 251

The whole pedigree’s bit size is 2 * 251 - 124 = 378.

shrunk <- shrinkPedigree(ped, genotyped, maxBits = 16L)
lengths(shrunk$idList)
#>   unavail noninform  affected 
#>       104         4       214
c(shrunk$pedSizeOriginal, shrunk$pedSizeIntermed, shrunk$pedSizeFinal)
#> [1] 375 267  53
shrunk$bitSize[c(1L, 2L, length(shrunk$bitSize))]
#> [1] 378 237  16

It works in steps. It first removes 104 unavailable animals: those not genotyped that are left with no offspring, and founders that add nothing. Then it removes 4 genotyped animals with no offspring left whose sire and dam are both genotyped. That takes the pedigree from 375 animals to 267, and its bit size from 378 to 237. Last, it removes one genotyped animal with no offspring left at a time, each time the one whose removal leaves the smallest bit size, with the animals that removal leaves unavailable, until the bit size is at most 16. That takes 214 more animals and leaves 53, at a bit size of 16. Its help page gives each rule.

Finding unrelated animals

findUnrelated() chooses genotyped animals of which no two are related, as many as it can: 44 of the 109 genotyped animals here. Their kinship coefficients with each other are all 0.

unrelated <- findUnrelated(ped, genotyped)
length(unrelated)
#> [1] 44
kU <- k[unrelated, unrelated]
all(kU[upper.tri(kU)] == 0)
#> [1] TRUE

For kinship2 users

asPedFrame() converts a kinship2 pedigree or pedigreeList, or a Pedixplorer Pedigree, to a list: the pedigree as a data frame (ped), its twins table (twinRelations) and its layout hints (hints), each NULL when the object has none. The chunks below run only when kinship2 is installed. They convert family 2 of kinship2’s sample.ped, 14 animals. kinship2 codes sex as 1 and 2 and an unknown parent as 0; the data frame has "M", "F" and NA.

data("sample.ped", package = "kinship2")
fam2 <- sample.ped[sample.ped$ped == 2, ]
p <- kinship2::pedigree(id = fam2$id, dadid = fam2$father,
                        momid = fam2$mother, sex = fam2$sex,
                        affected = fam2$affected)
x <- asPedFrame(p)
head(x$ped)
#>    id sire  dam sex affected
#> 1 201 <NA> <NA>   M        1
#> 2 202 <NA> <NA>   F       NA
#> 3 203 <NA> <NA>   M        1
#> 4 204  201  202   F        0
#> 5 205  201  202   M       NA
#> 6 206  201  202   F        1

The data frame then goes to the functions above, and kinship() gives the same coefficients as kinship2’s own kinship().

x$ped$gen <- findGeneration(x$ped$id, x$ped$sire, x$ped$dam)
k2 <- kinship(x$ped$id, x$ped$sire, x$ped$dam, x$ped$gen)
all.equal(k2, kinship2::kinship(p)[x$ped$id, x$ped$id])
#> [1] TRUE

Where next

?pedkindraw lists every function by what it does. vignette("drawing", package = "pedkindraw") shows what a drawing shows and how to change it, one feature at a time: the symbols and the legend, conditions, twins, animals drawn twice, the two edge styles and layout hints, among others. The help pages of makePedigreeMatingLayout() and drawPedigreeDiagram() describe the twins table, the kinship matrix and the layout hints the drawing takes.
